messages.body_plain:
Thanks very much for this advice. Items still had the same DIF estimates though, so based on that and your caution about DIF with bifactor, I decided to just do unidimensional DIF analysis for that part of the project. I really appreciate your help though.

Joe

On Friday, June 4, 2021 at 4:03:28 PM UTC-4 rphilip....@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Joe,
>
> There's a strong to good chance that bifactor models don't work super well with DIF, largely because of their identification constraints to perform the numerical integration efficiently. I don't prevent such inputs, but just want to warn you that care must be taken with these models as they are slightly more constrained at the outset than one might prefer....
>
> Anyway, in this particular case I don't think you want the 'drop' scheme, but rather the 'add' one. Drop is used when you have equality constraints set up across groups but want them removed to see if the model improves; 'add' is the converse, where the item's respective parameters are freely estimated across the groups but you now want to impose an equality constraint to see if the model gets worse. So, drop is looking to see if the model significantly improves (i.e., item has DIF), while add is looking to see if the model gets worse under the constraint (i.e., contains DIF...). A little confusing in the terminology, but both are sides of the same coin. HTH.
>
> Phil
>

Hi Phil

According to this example

set.seed(12345)
a <- matrix(abs(rnorm(15,1,.3)), ncol=1)

messages.body_plain:
Which scoring method are you using? A code snippet might help. Someone (Phil) can correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe this warning is generated when ML scores are based on response patterns where an infinite score would otherwise be produced (e.g., all "correct" or all "incorrect"). Convergence problems can also happen with ML and MAP scoring for other reasons. EAP scoring won't generate such a warning. But, depends on whether you want ML or MAP vs EAP for some reason.

messages.body_plain:
This is a question I have as well and its nice to see that people have addressed it already, thank you guys.

On Tuesday, September 21, 2021 at 11:24:55 PM UTC+3 rphilip....@gmail.com wrote:
> I'm not 100% sure what is being asked here, but in case this is just about how to obtain the associated parameters for a higher-order model after having fit a testlet model via bfactor() the result is reasonably straightforward. For the higher-order model the form is
>
> P(y|θ,ψ) = ∑ as θs + d
>
> where the θs terms are models according to the general factor θs = βs θg + ϵ. However, rather than fitting this model the testlet response model can be fit instead to impose the proportionality constraints, and then back-transformed when the model converges. Below is an example of this from the manual:
>
> ##########
> library(mirt)
>
> #simulate data
> set.seed(1234)
> a <- matrix(0, 12, 4)
> a[,1] <- rlnorm(12, .2, .3)
> ind <- 1
> for(i in 1:3){
>    a[ind:(ind+3),i+1] <- a[ind:(ind+3),1]
>    ind <- ind+4
> }
> print(a)
> d <- rnorm(12, 0, .5)
> sigma <- diag(c(1, .5, 1, .5))
> dataset <- simdata(a,d,2000,itemtype=rep('2PL', 12),sigma=sigma)
>
> # estimate by applying constraints and freeing the latent variances
> specific <- c(rep(1,4),rep(2,4), rep(3,4))
> model <- "G = 1-12
>           CONSTRAIN = (1, a1, a2), (2, a1, a2), (3, a1, a2), (4, a1, a2),
>             (5, a1, a3), (6, a1, a3), (7, a1, a3), (8, a1, a3),
>             (9, a1, a4), (10, a1, a4), (11, a1, a4), (12, a1, a4)
>           COV = S1*S1, S2*S2, S3*S3"
>
> simmod <- bfactor(dataset, specific, model)
> coef(simmod, simplify=TRUE)
> ####
>
> From this output the loadings on either the general of specific factor correspond to the same loadings as in the higher-order model (as they're constrained to be equal), while the β coefficients are obtained by way of the transformation 1/√{VAR(θs)). Using the above output, just use
>
> ###
> cov <- coef(simmod, simplify=TRUE)$cov
> betas <- 1 / sqrt(diag(cov)[-1L])
> betas
> ###
>
> HTH.
>
> Phil
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

Is it possible for the expected.test() to work for bifactor models?

I calculated the theta scores of the bifactor model and used the expected.test() to convert the theta scores back to raw scores. However, the estimated score range of the general factor is the same as the specific factor. I guess this is to be expected.

I've tried running a general factor model instead, but the M2 fit statistics are no good, and it's clearly a multidimensional model.

I wonder if there is a better way I could convert the theta estimates of the general factor back to the original scale (i.e. sum score of all items)

Kind regards,
Aiden

messages.subject: Re: Plot Expected Score to ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
You can compute expected item scores using the expected.item() function, then use these to build a plot:

set.seed(12345)
k_items <- 15
a <- matrix(abs(rnorm(k_items,1,.3)), ncol=1)
d <- matrix(rnorm(k_items,0,.7),ncol=1)
itemtype <- rep('2PL', k_items)

N <- 1000
dataset1 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype)
dataset2 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype, mu = .1, sigma = matrix(1.5))
dat <- rbind(dataset1, dataset2)

# ensure 'Ref' is the first group (and therefore reference group during estimation)
group <- factor(c(rep('Ref', N), rep('Focal', N)), levels = c('Ref', 'Focal'))

mod <- multipleGroup(dat, 1, group = group,
                     invariance = c(colnames(dat)[1:5], 'free_means', 'free_var'))
coef(mod, simplify=TRUE)

empirical_ES(mod)
